title: Prayer on the go
hook: A road trip, a hospital bed, no sink in sight. Prayer comes with you, and Allah made it easier for exactly these days.

screens.text: Prayer doesn't stay home when you travel, get sick, or can't find water. Allah made it lighter for those days, not optional. Today: four tools for real life.

variant.default: **Traveling.** On a long trip, the four-rak'ah prayers (Dhuhr, Asr, Isha) can be shortened to two, a gift from Allah [Q 4:101; Muslim 686]. Fajr, Maghrib and witr stay the same.
variant.hanafi: **Traveling.** Heading roughly 48–50 miles (77–81 km) or more away? Once you leave your town, pray Dhuhr, Asr and Isha as **two** rak'ahs, a gift from Allah [Q 4:101; Muslim 686]. Fajr, Maghrib and witr stay the same.
hanafi_bubbles: It lasts until you're home, or until you plan to stay **15 days or more** in one place.
Praying behind a local imam? Pray all four with him.

bubbles: {{masjid.name}} will tell you its rules: the distance, how long a stay counts, and combining prayers.

screens.prompt: You're on a long trip. Which prayers shorten?

items.why: A four-rak'ah prayer, so on a trip it becomes two [Q 4:101].
Fajr is already two. It stays the same.
Four rak'ahs at home, two on the road.
Four becomes two on a trip.
Witr isn't shortened. Pray it as you do at home.

screens.prompt: Luis drives 150 miles for a 3-day work conference. At the hotel, how does he pray Dhuhr?

options.feedback: Yes. A long trip and a short stay make him a traveler, so the four-rak'ah prayers become two.
Not quite. A traveler shortens Dhuhr, Asr and Isha to two.

options.text: He skips it and makes it up at home
options.feedback: Not quite. Travel makes prayer shorter, not skippable. Pray it on time, as two.

screens.text: **When you're sick.** The Prophet ﷺ told a man in pain: pray standing; if you can't, sitting; if you can't, lying on your side [Bukhari 1117].

screens.title: Praying when you're sick
screens.intro: Pray as you're able. Here's how it changes when you can't stand.

moves.text: Stand if you can. Sit only if standing would be truly hard or harmful, not just tiring.
Then sit, on the floor or a chair, and pray as you know how.
Can't bow or prostrate? Nod your head instead…
…and nod lower for prostration than for bowing [SeekersGuidance, sick person].
End with the salam, as in every prayer.

screens.done_text: Can't sit either? Pray lying on your side [Bukhari 1117].

variant.default: **No water? Tayammum.** No water nearby, or water would harm you? Use clean earth instead [Q 5:6]. **Tayammum** (dry purification) replaces wudu or ghusl until something breaks it, or water can be used.
variant.hanafi: **No water? Tayammum.** No water within about a mile, or water would harm you? Use clean earth instead [Q 5:6]. **Tayammum** (dry purification) replaces wudu or ghusl until something breaks it, or water can be used.

screens.title: How to do tayammum

steps.text: Intend it in your heart and say *Bismillah*
Strike your palms on clean earth

screens.done_text: {{masjid.name}} will show you its details: one strike or two, and how far up the arms.

steps.text: Intend it in your heart and say *Bismillah*
Strike your palms on clean earth or stone
Wipe your right arm up to and including the elbow, then your left

hanafi.done_text: Two strikes: face, then arms. Use it only when water isn't an option.

screens.prompt: Your turn: put tayammum in order.
items: Intend it in your heart and say Bismillah
Strike your palms on clean earth
screens.feedback: That's tayammum. Use it only when water isn't an option [Q 5:6].

items: Intend it in your heart and say Bismillah
Strike your palms on clean earth or stone
Wipe your right arm to the elbow, then your left
hanafi.feedback: That's tayammum: two strikes, face, then arms. Use it only when water isn't an option.

screens.situation: Destiny is in the hospital after surgery. She's hooked to an IV, can't get out of bed, and can't wet her bandaged arm.

options.text: Ask a nurse for the qibla and a basin of water. Wash what she can and wipe over the bandage, or do tayammum if she can't. Then pray in bed, nodding
options.feedback: Yes. She does what she can, the way she can. That's exactly what these rules are for.

options.text: Skip prayers until she's discharged, then make them all up
options.feedback: Not quite. Prayer stays due, but in a lighter form. Pray each one on time, however she can.

options.text: Pull out the IV so she can make full wudu
options.feedback: Please don't. Allah doesn't ask us to harm ourselves. Wiping over the bandage, tayammum and praying in bed are allowed for this.

variant.default: **Wiping over socks.** The Prophet ﷺ wiped over his footwear instead of washing his feet [Muslim 276]. {{masjid.name}} will tell you which socks count, so ask your imam before you rely on it.
variant.hanafi: **Wiping over socks.** Put on leather **khuffs** or thick socks you can walk in normally (they cover the ankles) after a full wudu. At your next wudu, wipe the top of each with wet fingers [Abu Dawud 162].
hanafi_bubbles: It lasts 24 hours at home, 3 days traveling [Muslim 276], counted from when your wudu breaks.
Ordinary thin socks don't count in our school.

Allah doesn't want hardship for you [Q 5:6]. Wherever you are, you can still pray.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Shortening is a gift from Allah [Q 4:101; Muslim 686]. **Hanafi:** a journey of about 48–50 miles (77–81 km; SeekersGuidance says 48 miles, the masjid's manual 81 km) makes you a traveler once you leave your city's boundary; shortening the four-rak'ah prayers to two is wajib; it continues until you return or intend to stay 15+ days in one place; Fajr, Maghrib and witr aren't shortened; a traveler behind a resident imam prays the full four [First Instructions on Worship; SeekersGuidance (Tabraze Azam): when one is a traveler; questions on travel prayer; traveler behind a resident imam]. The Hanafi school doesn't combine prayers outside Hajj (Day 5). Jumu'ah isn't required of travelers (Day 11).
- Illness: pray standing; if unable, sitting; if unable, on the side [Bukhari 1117]. Hanafi: standing drops only for real hardship; sitting however is easiest (floor or chair); if unable to bow and prostrate, nod, lower for sujud than ruku'; if unable to sit, lie down (on the back with feet toward the qibla, or on the side) and nod [SeekersGuidance, sick person's prayer (al-Kharsa)].
- Tayammum is allowed without water or when water would harm [Q 5:6]. Hanafi: intend, Bismillah, strike clean earth or anything of the earth's surface (stone counts), wipe the whole face; strike again, wipe the right arm including the elbow, then the left. Water about a mile away counts as unavailable. Same method for wudu or ghusl [SeekersGuidance, how to make tayammum (Tabraze Azam)]. It ends with whatever breaks wudu, and when water can be used.
- Bandages and casts (screen 10): wash what can be washed and wipe over the bandage; if most of the wudu limbs can't be washed, or no one can help bring water, tayammum (Hanafi). Keep it general; details go to the imam.
- Socks (Q12): wiping over footwear is established [Muslim 274; Muslim 276]; wipe the top [Abu Dawud 162]. Hanafi: khuffs, or thick socks that cover the ankle and can be walked in normally (the classical tests: stay up by themselves, don't let water through); worn after full wudu; 24h resident / 72h traveler counted from the first time wudu breaks after putting them on [Muslim 276; SeekersGuidance, thick socks; Qibla 37169]. Ordinary thin socks: not valid in the Hanafi school; AMJA allows them [AMJA 78081]. Don't resolve.

**Likely questions**
- *"Qibla on a plane / train?"* Face it at the start if you can; if not possible, pray as you can and ask the imam whether to repeat (details differ by school and situation).
- *"Can I pray in my car?"* Fard prayers are prayed on the ground where possible; stop if you can. Routes for long drives: plan stops. Edge cases go to the imam.
- *"Sunnahs while traveling?"* Encourage the 2 before Fajr and witr (witr is required in the Hanafi school and isn't shortened); route the rest to the imam.
- *"What counts as 'leaving town'?"* Past the city's built-up limits/boundary.
- *"My socks: do they count?"* Describe the Hanafi tests; if unsure, wash the feet. Mention scholars differ; offer "Ask my imam".
- *"I'm on my period / need ghusl and have no water."* Tayammum works for ghusl too; on a period, prayer isn't due until it ends.

**Escalate:** chronic illness and ongoing medical conditions (incontinence, constant bleeding: special Hanafi rules for the "excused person"); long work travel or students living away (residency questions); wiping over casts or bandages; combining prayers for anyone following another school; anything medical (a doctor decides what's safe).

**Don't**
- Don't teach wiping over thin cotton socks as the masjid default, and don't call AMJA's view invalid.
- Don't present shortening as optional in the Hanafi variant (it's required for a traveler).
- Don't tell anyone to risk their health to stand or use water.
- Don't give a fixed distance as if all schools agree.
madhabNote: Travel: the other three schools use a similar distance, but treat shortening as allowed rather than required, count a shorter stay as ending travel, and allow combining Dhuhr with Asr and Maghrib with Isha while traveling (Day 5). Tayammum: schools differ on one strike or two, and on wiping to the wrists or the elbows. Socks: see the madhab map; the Maliki school limits wiping to leather footwear, while the Hanbali school and AMJA are the most lenient.
